description: There are two very distinct morphotypes growing alongside each other at this location. The first (and apparently most widespread) type has leaflets toothed relatively shallowly with obtuse apices on the teeth, frequently with a short apiculus; the shape of the leaflets is generally elliptical to obovate, and the leaflets are distinctly pedicellate; the color of the apex of the petiole (where the leaflets are attached) is usually purplish, and the leaflets themselves often have a yellowish-green color. The second morphotype is featured in this observation and is apparently less widespread. It has coarsely and deeply toothed leaflets with teeth acute to acuminate and with a relatively long apiculus. The leaflets are strongly obovate and are sessile or subsessile, and the apex of the petiole is typically greenish in color. The leaflets themselves are dark green in coloration. This morphotype is apparently mostly restricted to nutrient-rich mesic forests and can be quite common in Central MS.

description:
Tropical Park pineland, one day post burn. A very small part at the southern end of the preserve was still burning but most of the fire was completely out/not hot. This is a pine rockland habitat, dependent on fire to keep the mostly open canopy consisting of only slash pine and the rich diversity of native grasses, shrubs and forbs as an understory. For more info about the importance of fire in pine rocklands, see here: https://www.miamidade.gov/environment/library/brochures/pine-rocklands.pdf
& here: https://www.miamidade.gov/environment/pine-rocklands.asp

This pineland had been taken over by many invasive plants due to fire suppression and unfortunately also infiltrated by cats (there are probably hundreds of cans of cat food in some parts of this preserve thanks to people feeding the cats). I am hoping to volunteer with EEL to help clean up and also pull up any invasive plants that pop up. I came back on Monday, May 17th, five days post burn, and noticed an area with lots of rosary pea (Abrus precatorius) dropping fruit/seed in part of the preserve.

It is unclear to me how the fire started but my understanding is the fire department came and initially was planning on putting the fire out (even hosing down some of it) but then thankfully let it burn out on its own. I thought I heard it was a prescribed burn but based on how the news reported on it, that doesn't seem to have been the case.

Link to news article about the fire: https://wsvn.com/news/local/miami-dade/part-of-tropical-park-catches-fire-near-soccer-field/

My goal here was to sort of map the burn via iNaturalist, showing the state of plants in different parts of the preserve. I was very careful not to bring any seeds in on my shoes/socks/clothes! I unfortunately really goofed and did not have my phone geotagging my observations. I had to estimate the locations so basically all of my work of photographing the plants did not work out the way I planned. My impression is that there was a substantial area that was not burned a bit west of the path that goes north/south through the preserve. I thought I was documenting the location but, again, I must've accidentally turned off the geotagging feature on my phone's camera. When I came back the following Monday (five days post burn), it seemed like this island of green had been burned, so I am wondering if EEL had a fire crew come out and burn areas that were leftover.

description: With usually 5 leaflets, occasionally 3–7 (1st photo all 7, 6th photo 3-6), radiating from the tip of the petiole, coarsely toothed, pointed tip, tapered to 6" long to the base, Virginia creeper (*Parthenocissus quinquefolia*) is closely related to and commonly confused with *Parthenocissus inserta*: differences include their means of climbing, the tendrils twining around plant stems in *P. inserta* lacking the round, adhesive discs that are found on tendril tips of *P. quinquefolia*, though the ends may be club-shaped when inserted into a crevice, with a consequence that (unlike *P. quinquefolia*) it cannot climb smooth walls, only shrubs and trees; young *P. inserta* leaflets are shiny and only slightly pale below, those of *P. quinquefolia* dull above and pale green, whitened, or glaucous below; *P. inserta* flowerhead branching is dichotomous or trichotomous, its branches of equal thickness, *P. quinquefolia* branches are unequal, with a definite central axis; the berries of *P. inserta* are larger, at 8–12 mm in diameter, *versus* 5–8 mm broad in *P. quinquefolia*; petiolules of mature *P. inserta* leaflets are typically longer, 5–30 mm long, *versus* sessile (or to 10 mm) as displayed here in *P. quinquefolia*

description:
5 leaflets on a palmately compound leaf

It's a creeper (creeps up existing tree, unlike grabbers like grape or constrictors like Japanese honeysuckle), meaning thickly hairiness attaches this vine to the tree or whatever it is climbing

Productive fruit producer. Important food for autumn bird migration 

Branches are short

Winter ID:

-The hairs/aerial rootlets are much thicker than the poison ivy hairs; die back when vine is old

-Bark is brown (PI bark is black), and corky

-Circular leaf scars and buds

Virginia Creeper is considered a Native plant but it can also be an Invasive depending on the situation. Virginia creeper grows all over in the forest and covers many things such as fences,trees,and other objects. This plant disrupts many things in the forest and other objects near the plant. Virginia creeper meets two of the basic needs for survival which is cover and food. The different species that eat the berries off of the vine includes squirrels, mice, deer, chipmunks, mockingbirds, nuthatches, woodpeckers and blue jays. This plant provides a very dense cover and as result it stunts the growth of many different species of plants in the area because they have very little access to sunlight. This is something we DO NOT NEED and the best management practices to remove this is by Uprooting the plant, burning it with fire, and using chemicals such as roundup.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; our first visit -- but probably not our last -- because Don Fraser advised us on a "sure-thing" spot for Hayhurst's Scallopwing (we found 16+!).

We drove the entire loop (14 miles) and I separated our observations into three areas: 1; here) the loop, various generic locations; 2; the scallopwing spot) the kiosk area at the northwestern corner of the loop; and 3) the corral where they put the pregnant cows (with lots of spilled feed for icterids).

We entered the WMA at 1010 and drove the main loop counter-clockwise, arriving at the kiosk area at 1050 and remaining there until 1304), when we continued south then east along the loop (the panther encounter was at 1316). We reached the corral at 1351 and remained there until 1359. We exited the WMA at 1422. The weather at the start was sunny and 80 degrees with a light breeze; it was a few degrees warmer by the time we left.

I hesitate to mention this observation, since it is not supported by photographs, but Val and I saw what we presume was a Florida Panther (!). It appeared to have been lying in the road south of the kiosk when we spotted it at 1316. We were maybe 500 feet away when we saw an object in the road. It got up, facing us, and was an obvious feline. Val asked, "Bobcat?" but then it started moving off the road to its right (our left) and I remarked, "It has a long tail." At that point, I grabbed for my camera (sitting in my lap) -- I don't remember if I even put the car in park -- and fired off three photographs as quickly as possible, shot through the Camry's windshield. Even though such photos are typically really blurry, I had no other option. Unfortunately, the cat had slinked off the road by the time I hit the shutter (a duration of probably 5 seconds). So, no photos. I was speechless for several minutes before Val and I started discussing what we saw. It was an obvious cat bigger than a fox and maybe smaller than a Coyote, with a long tail maybe 14-16 inches long. It was pale tawny overall; we saw no radio collar

I don't know if panthers are found outside cover during the middle of the day -- especially on a day with youth hunting of Wild Turkeys occurring -- I would think not usually, but the size of the cat and its obviously long tail rule out other species other than an escaped/released cougar or other subspecies of Felis concolor. It was exciting, but since it happened so fast and especially because I got no photographs, I'm not really sure how I feel about it.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo. An unexpected trip south from a job in Lakeland via meeting the crew in Tampa at 0530. Val texted me that the Black-billed Cuckoo found yesterday at Pinecraft Park in Sarasota was seen again this morning, and she was going for it when she got off work at noon. She found the cuckoo -- a lifer! -- by 1315 and called me. I headed down from Tampa and Val showed me the cuckoo, which was extremely cooperative, almost immediately. It was a photographic lifer for me; Black-billed Cuckoo is a surprisingly tough bird in Florida; I've seen only three or four in 40+ years of birding the state. The weather at the start was sunny, 83 degrees ("feels like" 87), and breezy. We left at  1558 and headed to Gecko's Grill for dinner. I got home at 2106.

Because I had no optics with me, I used Val's camera to take these images. Val's camera tends to take slightly unfocused photographs more often than focused photographs, for some inexplicable reason. Oh well ... Plus, the lighting was pretty dreadful, so many of my images are intentionally overexposed to show detail in the subjects.

The weather at the start was partly cloudy, 87 degrees ("feels like" 95), and breezy. We did not visit Cedars of Lebanon Cemetery. We left at 1438 and headed to Applebee's' in Crystal River for delicious lunches of cheeseburgers.

Note: the dial on my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 that controls exposure "broke" (i.e., ceased working) just before we left Big Cypress Boardwalk at Goethe State Forest. I can no longer adjust the exposure in the camera, and I do not believe in editing my photographs unless absolutely necessary. The exposure setting the camera is now "stuck on" is pretty nice (not too dark, not too light), but I would have turned down the exposure 1/2-1 "f-stop" if the exposure setting was still working. Other than cropping, I did not alter photograph here.

A solo visit because I hadn't been here in two months. I walked the northern loop of the nature trail to the powerlines, then followed them northeast to the northern fenceline, then wound my way through the May 2023 burn to the west fenceline, then back west to Jet. The May 2023 burn was full of passionflower and other plants, which formed a dense mat above the ground -- good thing I'm not wary of snakes! I was surprised to see that the Clusterspike False Indigo plants are again blooming -- I'm guessing due to the recent burn; there was lots of insect activity on the flowers. The burn was loaded with Mocis and similar moths, various yellows and sulphurs (6 species if iNat is correct!), and Gulf Fritillaries -- I could have spent all days photographing passionflower and fritillaries. I found 5 chrysalises in the burn or attached to the barbed-wire fence to the north; I'm guessing they were all fritillaries. I again recorded Northern Flicker calls, but still have yet to see a flicker here! The best surprise was a singing male Blue Grosbeak in the northeast corner of the May 2023 burn. The weather at the start was sunny, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), with calm winds. The weather at the end was sunny, 86 degrees ("feels like" 100), with calm winds. There was no humidity overnight; all the vegetation was dry. I left at 0957.

description:
A visit after work; only my second visit here -- the first was years ago -- to see if I could find any butterflies or moths. I walked around the southern boundary all the way to Cliff Stephens Park, then walked the northern boundary back to Jet. There were TONS of small moths, caterpillars, and a pupae in oaks and other hardwood shrubs and trees along the northern boundary, while the southern boundary had some blooming (Joe) Bidens that attracted several butterflies. I tried to photograph every moth food plant in case some species are not known to be moth hosts, as well as to hopefully narrow down the moth identification possibilities. Moths were so abundant that walking by nearly every low-growing oak meant that 4, 5, 6, or more moths would fly out. Some landed on my shirt, pants, or hand! I also found a super-cool leafhopper that hopefully can be identified to species.

The park seemed to include centuries-old pines (I think Longleaf Pine but I'm not positive) and Live Oaks; I was not expecting either.

As this is an urban park, there were many exotic plants growing in it. However, I believe that none were intentionally planted -- rather, they naturalized -- so that all plants should be Research-Gradable.

I used my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 for all non-macro photographs, and I used my Samsung A52 cell phone for macro-photography.

I walked around the southern boundary all the way to Cliff Stephens Park, then walked the northern boundary back to Jet. There were TONS of small moths, caterpillars, and a pupae in oaks and other hardwood shrubs and trees along the northern boundary, while the southern boundary had some blooming (Joe) Bidens that attracted several butterflies. I tried to photograph every moth food plant in case some species are not known to be moth hosts, as well as to hopefully narrow down the moth identification possibilities. Moths were so abundant that walking by nearly every low-growing oak meant that 4, 5, 6, or more moths would fly out. Some landed on my shirt, pants, or hand! I also found a super-cool leafhopper that hopefully can be identified to species.

The park seemed to include centuries-old pines (I think Longleaf Pine but I'm not positive) and Live Oaks; I was not expecting either.

As this is an urban park, there were many exotic plants growing in it. However, I believe that none were intentionally planted -- rather, they naturalized -- so that all plants should be Research-Gradable.

I used my Panasonic Lumix FZ80 for all non-macro photographs, and I used my Samsung A52 cell phone for macro-photography.

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 73 degrees ("feels like" 73) with a light breeze. I left around 1635 and battled traffic all the way home.

description:
Southern Pinellas County butterfly count with Clint Gibson. We covered two areas (with multiple stops at each); the northern Sunshine Skyway causeway and Pinellas Point Park/Katherine B. Tippetts Park.

The Sunshine Skyway causeway is manmade and is vegetated with mangroves, Australian-pines, and a diversity of native and exotic shrubs, grasses, forbs. One of the native forbs, Annual Seepweed, is the host plant for the Western Pygmy-Blue, a butterfly discovered in Florida in the Tampa Bay area in 2021. We counted/estimated 860 Western Pygmy-Blues in a few acres here!

Pinellas Point Park and Katherine B. Tippetts Park (essentially the easternmost 1-2 acres of Pinellas Point Park) are several acres along Tampa Bay, vegetated with mangroves along the water (except where removed by homeowners to see the water), with 50-150 feet of mowed grass before meeting the boundary of private yards. The non-grass vegetation consists of a mix of native and exotic trees and shrubs, and native forbs. I was careful to avoid selecting any individual plant that was planted at some point in the past.

Our schedule was:

0900-1037: the western portion of the northern Skyway causeway, part of Skyway Fishing Pier State Park.

1042-1220: the eastern portion of the northern Skyway causeway, west of Skyway Beach, mostly along the paved road east of the north access lanes to Interstate 275. This is a strip of unmowed vegetation 5-30 feet wide and 0.5 miles long (north to the barricades in the road) that is grown abundantly to various low, flowering plants. We counted more than 100 Southern Skipperlings here! 

1235-1410: Pinellas Point Park/Katherine B. Tippets Park; mostly the former site.

Clint and I ended our count at 1410 and Clint returned me to my car at Skyway Bridge Rest Area.

1441-1541: I thought that I had lost my field notebook somewhere on the Skyway causeway, so I returned to our two sites and spent an hour looking for the notebook, mostly on the eastern side of Interstate 275. I was mostly concerned with finding my notebook, but I did take some photographs. Many Southern Skipperlings were perched on the vegetation, "airplaining" with their wings held out. I could have photographed a few dozen individuals if I had wanted to.

On my way home, I stopped at a Taco Bell for dinner, and I found my notebook inside my wallet. I always place my notebook in my right rear pocket, so I can't explain how it ended up in my right front pocket. But I'm happy it was there!

description:
With Don Fraser; a visit to see what was around. There was a lot of water around! The weather at the start was sunny and 88 degrees, with a light breeze (I had no cell phone reception, so I got the temperature from Don's SUV; the "feels like" temperature was probably 88-90 degrees), We drove North Grade Road, spent some time at the (graffiti-laden!) wooden bridge over the Little Withlacoochee River, then turned "left" onto River Road. We took River Road to County Road 471, then drove south back to North Grade Road, which we drove again to the bridge over the Little Withlacoochee River. We left around 1400, when the weather was sunny and hot (probably with a "feels like" temperature >100 degrees), with a light breeze. On the way back, we stopped at the Richloam General Store for refreshments.

I will upload "snips" of my (non-GPS-enabled) camera photographs at a later date. In some cases, I will replace the inferior cell-phone images of some species with superior camera images.

description: A skipper trip with Linda Cooper, Don Fraser, Clint Gibson, John Lampkin et al. -- unfortunately very underwhelming due to the lack of sunshine. We started at the campground along Center Grade (0924-1116) then continued east until we turned north onto North Grade and drove west to the wooden bridge over the Little Withlacoochee River. We had no cell phone service, so I could not check the weather, but it was overcast for the entire visit minus about 10 minutes near the end. The temperature at the start was 82 and extremely humid -- vegetation was dripping water -- and the temperature at the end was 87 (with a "feels like" temperature probably in the mid-90s). We left at 1330. Skippers were infrequent -- and we saw nothing rare -- but treefrogs and large ground-dwelling moths were crazy-abundant at the campground.
